To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
in hypertensive patients the coronary arteries dilate less than in control subjects in response to sympathetic stimuli, and that they do not dilate in response flow stimuli.

in hypertensive patients the cold pressor-induced sympathetic activation results in an increase in coronary blood flow velocity and a decrease in coronary diameter; in contrast, in control subjects the cold pressor induces an increase in coronary diameter and coronary blood flow.
the coronary arteries of hypertensive patients do not dilate in response the sympathetic stimulation induced by the cold presser test.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the coronary responses to sympathetic stimulation (induced by the cold presser test) and to flow-dependent vasodilation in normotensive subjects and in hypertensive patients (without coronary heart disease) with normal coronary arteries.
the study of the coronary vasodilatory responses in hypertensive patients without coronary artery disease.
the study of the coronary responses to sympathetic stimulation and to papaverine-induced hyperemia in hypertensive patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
in hypertensive patients the coronary vasodilatory response to cold pressor test was similar to that of control subjects.
the coronary vasodilatory responses of the cold pressor stimulus and of the intracoronary injection of papaverine are altered in hypertensive patients.

the coronary responses to cold pressor test and to intracoronary papaverine were similar in hypertensive patients and normal control subjects, but the coronary vasodilator responses to cold presser were impaired in hypertensive patients.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have demonstrated that the coronary vascular response to cold pressor testing is blunted in patients with hypertension and angiographically normal coronary artery.
the coronary arteries of hypertensive patients with normal coronary arteries have a reduced ability to vasodilate in response to both sympathetic and flow-dependent stimuli.
in hypertensive patients without angiographically demonstrable coronary artery disease, coronary vasodilator reserve is decreased.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the coronary arteries of hypertensive patients do not dilate normally, either in response to cold pressor test-induced sympathetic stimulation or to papaverine-induced flow increase, and this may be related to the presence of coronary atherosclerosis.
the cold pressor stress test is a useful tool for the evaluation of coronary vasomotor function in patients with angiographically documented CAD.
there are two different types of coronary artery disease, one that is related to atherosclerosis and the other that is not.
